# Beware of Cutting Down

> "But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts."
>
> — Romans 13:14

Sooner or later almost every man in the trap tries a ration.

Sometimes he means it as a stepping stone: "I'll ease off gradually, and then I'll stop." Sometimes he means it as a truce with the Little Monster: "I'll never be rid of you, so let's agree terms." It nearly always arrives after a failed attempt to stop outright. A few days in, the man cracks, and the next morning he says something like this:

"Never again is too much to ask. So from now on it's Saturdays only. Or only in the shower. Or only from my own head, with no screen. If I can hold it there for a while, I'll trim it further, and one day it will just fade out."

If you quit porn before you picked up this book, you may notice that you're living on one of these deals already. "Only without porn" is a ration too. One man on the NoFap forum tried exactly that deal for Lent, porn out and the habit kept, and found what it was worth: "I noticed I couldn't MO without thinking about P".

It sounds like the moderate, grown-up option. Of everything a man can try, it is the worst, and it's the reason plenty of men stay caught for life. Here is what happens to him.

1. **He gets the worst of both worlds.** He's still feeding the Little Monster, so the itch never dies. He's also thinking about the habit more than he ever did, so the Big Monster grows fat as well.
2. **He wishes his life away.** Monday to Friday become a corridor he has to walk down. He's a grown man counting sleeps.
3. **He carries the itch all week.** Before the ration, when the urge came he gave in, and the restlessness at least eased for a while. Now he drags it through six days out of seven, on top of everything else life hands him. He gets short with his wife and kids and can't think why.
4. **Every time becomes "special".** Before, most of the times were automatic. He barely noticed them, and he certainly didn't treasure them. Now that he has waited six days, Saturday night feels like Christmas.

Look hard at number four, because the whole trick is in it. The relief was never in the act. The relief is the itch ending. So the longer the itch is left to nag, the bigger the relief seems, and the surer he is that he's enjoying something. He has turned a dull routine into a treat by making himself suffer for it first.

## The flesh was never the hard part {-}

Remember the smoker on the plane. You've gone a week at your in-laws, or ten days on a mission trip sharing a room, and hardly given it a thought. There was no chance of it, so the Little Monster kept quiet.

Now try the same ten days at home, alone, with the door shut and nobody due back, telling yourself you mustn't. You'd be chewing the furniture by Wednesday.

Your body is the same in both cases. The difference is whether it's on offer. And on a ration it is always on offer, because Saturday is always coming. The monster never gets the message that the kitchen has closed. He just learns the opening hours, and he sits by the door all week.

Most men secretly like the stretches when it's impossible: the house full of guests, the camping trip, the fortnight sharing a room. There's a small pride in it. "Look at that, eight days, and I was fine." It gives them hope that one day they won't want it at all. That hope is sound. It's the ration that kills it.

The hard part of stopping was never the flesh. It's the lie: the belief that the habit is a comfort or a reward, something you're owed, and that life would be thinner without it. Cutting down does nothing to that lie except feed it. A man on a ration ends up convinced that the most precious thing in his week is five minutes on a Saturday night. He set out to make the habit smaller, and he has made it the centre of his calendar.

## Less is not less {-}

Few things are sadder than the man who believes that the less he does it, the less he'll want it.

The reverse is true. The less he does it, the longer the itch runs, and the sweeter the scratching feels. He'll also find that the old favourites have stopped working so well, and that he "needs" something a little stronger to make the long wait worth it. That is how a man who swore he'd only ever use his imagination ends up back on his phone.

Hard to believe? Then answer two questions.

What is the hardest part of the week for a Saturdays-only man? The six days of waiting.

And what is the best moment of his week? Saturday night, which is the moment the six days of waiting end.

So which is it? Is he doing it for the joy of the thing? Or is he ending a misery the habit gave him, and calling it a reward he has earned?

You can test this on yourself without changing anything. (You're still carrying on as normal until the book is finished. No rations for you either.) Just think back. Take the days you did it twice. How was the second time? Flat and pointless, more than likely. Now think of a time you'd gone ten days without and then gave in. Fireworks.

The act was the same. Your hand was the same. The memory you used may well have been the same. The only thing that changed was how long you'd been kept waiting. If a thing were truly good, it would still be good the second time. A second helping of roast potatoes is still roast potatoes.

That's why the rationed time looks so much better than the daily one. There's no real pleasure in either. What separates them is only how miserable you were beforehand.

## Willpower for life {-}

So cutting down doesn't work. It's also a slow kind of torture.

It doesn't work because it rests on a hope: do a thing less and less, and the wish for it will shrink. That's how ordinary habits behave, and this isn't an ordinary habit. An appetite that is fed, even a little, comes back asking for more. It never asks for less. So to hold the line at once a week, a man has to push back against the pull with willpower and discipline, and he has to keep pushing every day until he dies.

**CUTTING DOWN MEANS WILLPOWER FOR LIFE.**

If you had that kind of willpower to spare, you'd have stopped years ago. Stopping completely is far easier, and it hurts far less.

The same goes for every half-measure dressed up as progress. Edging is one: a man goes right up to the end and stops, tells himself "at least I didn't finish", and has in fact kept the engine running for an hour. Looking without touching is another. So is touching without looking. So is "just checking". A man who had read EasyPeasy confessed how he used to cheat on his own rules: "Sometimes I only 'checked' if my body response for touch." They're all rations. One man who'd tried the first of them left this for the men coming after him:

> "Don't edge. Really. Don't do it. It's the absolutely worst thing to do."
>
> — a man on a porn-recovery site

A pastor writing about this habit reached the same place from the other direction: "Most people cannot conquer lust until they stop masturbating for a time". He doesn't say cut down. He says stop. The counsellor Heath Lambert, writing about porn, set out the choice more starkly still: "Employing radical measures is the path to life, while indulging sin is the path to hell." A ration is indulgence with a timetable.

The newest ration comes with a medical label. Men whose bodies have stopped answering to a real woman, the trouble described a few chapters ago, are sometimes advised to "retrain" with a gentler, slower version of the same habit. It's cutting down by another name. A woman on the NoFap forum watched a man she loved try it: "if he moed no matter how light he would struggle in bed and so he needed to stop completely". He didn't want to, and she ended it. Her summary of the choice in front of such men is five words long: "MO or a healthy relationship".

Under one man's testimony a commenter wrote, in capitals, the sentence this whole chapter is trying to say: "GOD TOLD ME I COULDN'T KILL SOMETHING I CONTINUE TO FEED!"

Yes, a handful of men have cut down for a short while and then stopped for good. They got free in spite of the ration. All it did was stretch out the misery. For everyone else, each failed ration leaves a man a bit more rattled and a bit more certain he's a lifer, and that certainty is usually enough to send him back for another round.

## What cutting down does prove {-}

It's useful in one way. Cutting down shows you, more clearly than anything else could, that there's nothing in the habit. You only "enjoy" it after going without. You have to stand out in the cold for an hour to make coming indoors feel like a holiday.

So your choices are these:

1. Ration it for life, and put yourself through that every week. You won't manage it anyway.
2. Drop the ration, go back to doing it whenever, and let it take a bit more from you each year. Pointless.
3. Be kind to yourself and cut it out altogether.

Cutting down proves something else too: the "occasional one" doesn't exist. Each time sets up the next. It's a chain, and it will run to the end of your life unless you break it.

This is what Paul is getting at in the verse that opens the chapter. A ration is a provision. It's a standing reservation for the flesh: table for one, every Saturday, name on the list. Paul doesn't say to make a smaller provision. He says to make none.

Augustine, you'll remember, prayed for chastity, "only not yet". A ration is that prayer with a diary attached.

Remember:

**DON'T CUT IT DOWN. CUT IT OUT.**
